items.title: Show HN: Zeus – Claude Code for AI voice agents
items.summary: Hi everyone, Alex here - I’m one of the founders of ThunderPhone. We’re excited to announce the launch of Zeus, a platform that makes AI phone calls actually work without extensive hand-tuning! You can see a head-to-head I made of the last version of ThunderPhone vs this one here: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=YlkIc3L29lo A (somewhat long) summary: When we started building business phone agents in 2024, we kept running into technical problems that ruined calls, caused by the limits of existing architectures. The two biggest issues were that phone agents misheard callers, and disobeyed scripts or responded in weird ways. Both stemmed from the prevailing voice agent architecture - a “three-step” or “cascaded” pipeline: one transcription model turning caller audio into text, one LLM generating a response (and sometimes tool calls) from that text, and a TTS model turning response text into audio. Transcription models aren’t perfect, especially in noisy environments, with unclear callers, in languages other than English, and on short utterances like “yeah”. With the pipeline approach, when caller audio is boiled down to a single “best guess” text transcript, mistakes are often unrecoverable: there’s typically no “top n” best guesses or other audio signal for the LLM to use if the transcript was wrong. That leads the LLM to respond to what the transcription model thought it heard instead of what the caller actually said. The pipeline approach also caused weird responses and poor instruction-following due to the tradeoff between LLM speed and intelligence. Phone calls demand fast responses to feel natural, which is in tension with an LLM’s need to “think” and run inference - often for several seconds - to answer many prompts correctly. With a single LLM in the pipeline, the obvious choice is picking one fast enough to feel responsive, but that comes with an unavoidably high error rate on real calls, frustrating callers and sending calls off the rails. More recently, end-to-end “speech-to-speech” models have won usage alongside three-step pipelines. They’re better at hearing callers correctly (though still not perfect), but they’re even worse at following instructions reliably, which is typically disastrous for business phone calls. Once we understood these problems, we built our own stack to address them. Over the past year and a half, the ThunderPhone stack has largely solved mishearing and misbehaving by combining numerous models on each call. For audio misunderstandings, we run multiple, even numerous, transcription models on most calls, giving more “shots on goal” from the original audio. Even if none gets it exactly right, multiple almost-correct answers let us triangulate on a correct transcript, using one or more LLMs to decide what the caller actually said. In challenging situations, we even pipe caller audio directly to one or more audio-input LLMs to further improve comprehension. For instruction following, we run a mix of fast and slow LLMs on conversation turns to combine snappy responses with deeper thinking behind the scenes. In practice, this is a multi-staged classification problem: after 50ms, 500ms, 1s, etc., we simultaneously generate responses with increasing inference while classifying whether we need to “think harder” to generate a definitive correct answer. Together with other smaller optimizations, these two approaches have been very effective. Qualitatively, customer calls go much more smoothly and reach successful outcomes far more frequently than on three-step or speech-to-speech pipelines. Quantitatively, we’ve set a record of 99.4% on the Big Bench Audio benchmark, smarter than any other model fast enough for real calls. (We’re also benchmarking ThunderPhone on more public benchmarks - stay tuned.) The downside is configuration complexity. Every agent benefits from a different setup on the ThunderPhone stack, and even individual call turns on the same call often benefit from different stacks. Configuring this manually worked for enterprise customers, but made it prohibitive to give smaller self-serve customers the full benefits without giving their agents our full attention. That’s how Zeus came about. Our enterprise configurations were repetitive enough that an AI could do them once we taught it how and gave it the right tools. We’re big fans of Claude Code and Codex for software development, but they fall short at configuring voice agents for a few reasons. First, unlike software development, where you can compile code and run tests to verify things work, you can’t run live calls inside a computer right after configuring a voice agent - and coding agents don’t know how to run simulated calls out of the box, or “listen” to a call to spot real problems. We built both capabilities into Zeus, giving it a “closed loop” experience building, testing, and improving voice agents just like coding agents have with regular software. Second, coding agents are pretty gullible about marketing claims. Companies building AI and voice infrastructure commonly post the most favorable possible interpretation of their capabilities online. Claude and Codex read those claims, believe them uncritically, and pick tools based on marketing rather than real performance. At best, that leads to suboptimal architectural choices; at worst, to voice agents that don’t really work at all. We’ve sidestepped this with continuous evals feeding an internal knowledge base. For everything that matters for voice agents - accurate audio understanding, instruction following, noise cancelling, turn-taking, and more - we maintain internal benchmarks built on real call data. Every time a new AI model comes out, we (now mostly automatically) feed it through our evals for performance, speed, cost, and reliability/consistency. That feeds our internal knowledge base, which Zeus uses to pick the right stack for every agent, call, and conversation turn. This all happens behind the scenes to keep the ThunderPhone experience seamless. A user just describes their use case and goals, and Zeus helps fill in ambiguities, connect VoIP and software integrations, and optimize the voice agent(s) on simulated and live calls until they hit the highest performance on business goals (conversions, unit economics, etc.) possible with today’s models. Zeus is also differentiated on cost. Zeus itself is free to use for now, though we expect to move to subscription or token-based pricing later. For calls, we’ve become the first voice AI vendor to our knowledge to charge on a cost-plus basis: ThunderPhone customers pay exactly what we pay our vendors, plus a 17% margin on calls costing 2c/min or less, scaling linearly up to 25% for calls costing us 15c/min or more, and 25% from there on up. However, we find that simple phone agents do well on a stack that costs about 2c/min, and more complex cases typically land around 5-10c/min - significantly cheaper than most alternatives. Zeus is brand-new, so we’re eager to get feedback on how it works for customers, and any areas we could improve it. Give it a try and see what you think - let me know if you have any feedback or questions. Alex

items.title: TideCache: Efficient Hybrid LLM Serving with Transparent Cache Management and Layer-Wise Streaming
items.summary: Hybrid architectures have become mainstream among open-weight language models. Their global-attention and bounded-state layers maintain heterogeneous caches whose demands vary with context length and concurrency. We present TideCache, a serving system on CPU--GPU superchips with three components for allocating GPU memory among caches and managing their residency across GPU and host memory. The Transparent Cache Pool redistributes physical pages among cache components behind fixed virtual addresses, preserving cache layouts and backend interfaces. The Cache Streamer uses computation intervals provided by bounded-state layers to prefetch the next global-attention layer's prefix into GPU slots shared across global-attention layers, reducing GPU residency while overlapping layer-wise transfers with computation. Generated KV remains resident. The Request Scheduler selects resident or streamed execution and triggers capacity adjustments according to request size and queue state. Together, they let HBM released by streaming accommodate other cache components and additional requests. Implemented in SGLang and evaluated on GB300 and GH200 across seven model/platform configurations, TideCache completes up to 2.04x as many agent turns, reduces overall P50 per-token latency by 20--59%, and improves agent P50 TTFT by 1.40--3.05x compared with SGLang with HiCache.

items.title: Text-Aware, Vision-Blind: How Multimodal Image Editing Systems Handle Unsafe Inputs
items.summary: Multimodal image generation systems have made rapid progress and increasingly emphasize content safety. However, their safety mechanisms tend to rely on a single modality and lack joint consideration of both visual content and text prompts, particularly in instruction-guided image editing, where the uploaded image may itself carry risk. We thus introduce EditSafetyBench, a benchmark that measures system-level safety awareness of advanced image editing systems, containing 5,940 image-instruction pairs, covering safe and unsafe images across 11 risk categories and three edit intents. We then probe the benchmark dataset on four systems, including Gemini, GPT, Qwen API, and Qwen Local. Based on our evaluation, we observe a systematic text-vision safety mismatch: Gemini and GPT refuse 87.1\% and 81.6\% cases containing unsafe-intent editing prompts, while only refusing 24.2\% and 22.4\% cases with both unsafe images and neutral instructions. At the category level, most risks are considered inconsistently by different systems, e.g., GPT allows 70.4\% editing attempts of unsafe political content while Gemini only allows 34.8\%. Notably, sexual content shows the strongest visual sensitivity, likely benefiting from mature NSFW identification works. Our findings highlight the need for safety guardrails that jointly reason over both visual and textual modalities in image editing systems.

items.summary:
New Features

  • Added GPT-6.2 Sol and Astra to model catalogs, with Sol as the default catalog selection. (#62106)
  • Enabled the TUI workspace by default, with searchable document previews, image previews, and subagent transcripts alongside the main conversation. (#61352, #61888, #61889, #61919, #62157)
  • Added configurable undo and redo shortcuts to the non-Vim prompt composer, including restoration of attachments and large pastes. (#61954)
  • Added codex exec --remote <ADDR> to start or resume noninteractive sessions on an existing app server. (#61707)
  • Added /rc and /remote to manage local remote control and display device pairing codes from the TUI. (#62121)
  • Added custom MCP status line selection and authoring through /statusline when tui_extensions_statusline is enabled. (#61979, #61988, #62037)

Bug Fixes

  • Preserved drafts, queued follow-ups, and interrupted input with their original threads when switching or resuming sessions. (#61216)
  • Kept permission profiles intact when changing working directories. (#61195)
  • Prevented late completion events from cancelling approvals for a newer turn. (#61801)
  • Preserved earlier edits in aggregate diffs when steering an active turn. (#61820)
  • Fixed scrolling that inserted stray characters, composer caret jumps, and redraws using stale terminal dimensions. (#62139, #62174, #62175)
  • Fixed enterprise MCP sign-in for identity providers that issue ID tokens without refresh tokens. (#62129)

Chores

  • Updated source builds and release tooling to Rust 1.99.1. (#61205)
  • Updated XML dependencies and removed obsolete security advisory exceptions. (#62068)

items.title: Token fraud is here and it’s BAD (YouTube)
items.summary:
Token fraud is here and it’s BAD (YouTube)

Claire Vo runs ChatPRD, an AI platform that helps product managers "turn an idea into a spec". The product has been live since the GPT-4 era, and Claire has been building it in public for much of that time.

In this YouTube video (see also the accompanying Twitter post) Claire describes the flood of token fraud she has seen from groups abusing the product's free trial, sometimes just to get free AI usage but often to resell tokens or run other commercial enterprises on top of the ChatPRD agent.

I am funding a international Roblox and Fortnite map studio. They run a loop of free trials and promo codes and then tunnel to my agent and use it to build Roblox and Fortnite maps.

Apparently one of the common prompts Claire saw running through her agent involved SVGs of pelicans riding bicycles! Presumably the token scammers are using that to help sniff the underlying models - different model families have a definite signature, and I've used it like this in the past to try and guess the identity of stealth preview models on platforms like OpenRouter.

Claire is winding down her free trials entirely, which sadly looks like the right decision in the face of this abuse.

items.content_excerpt: How end-to-end, property and differential tests let coding agents verify their work with evidence, and what the Claude Code team does to keep its verifiers honest. On the Claude Code team, the vast majority of our code (~90%) is written and reviewed by Claude . At this scale, how we equip our agents to verify their work with evidence becomes extremely important. Verification loops are the building block that lets you delegate more work to Claude. Without them, you can really only run one or two Claudes at a time, because you have to check everything yourself. With them, you can run dozens or hundreds in parallel. That’s because giving agents a way to verify their output is an effective way to improve quality. In internal testing around structured file generation, having a separate grader check Claude’s work against a rubric improved task success by up to 10 points over a standard prompting loop, with the largest gains on the hardest problems. What was once expensive to verify (tests, benchmarks, specs, real end-to-end runs) is now cheap to request from an agent. Like code, agents can quickly generate tests, benchmarks, and specs. And once generated, these tests and benchmarks run as software so they can be run frequently without using many additional tokens. You can also close the verification loop by using the results to improve the agent’s performance on that task. For example, if an agent repeatedly fails a test that checks logs for user data, you can create a hook or a more explicit rule in your CLAUDE.md to avoid future issues. This (mostly) stops issues from happening again. So if verification is critical to producing quality code at a high velocity, what types of tests should you use and how should you apply them across your pipeline? This article answers those questions and also shares the process used by the Claude Code team. If your tests are flaky you’ll train the agent to run them again rather than fixing the failing code. If your tests are slow, the agent will do fewer tests across batches which can make pinpointing issues difficult. Heavier tests are best deployed before you’ve committed the changes. If you have to focus on one test type, pick end-to-end. These tests describe real user flows like adding an item to a cart, checking out, and moving to a confirmation page. items.title: External sandboxes for coding agents
items.summary:
External sandboxes for coding agents

I've been exploring new ways to sandbox code that is executed by agents, with a focus on making it safer to try out local models without worrying that a mistake or prompt injection attack might cause them to take damaging actions on a machine.

I worked on this project with Prime Radiant, the AI research lab behind Superpowers and other projects.

My post on the Prime Radiant blog introduces the external sandbox pattern, where code executed by the agent runs inside a dedicated sandbox while the agent itself lives outside of that sandbox.

To demonstrate this pattern we've released three sandbox server implementations:

  • external-sandbox-v86 runs a Node.js server which then uses v86 to run Alpine Linux inside WebAssembly.
  • external-sandbox-container is a Python web server which runs the sandbox in Alpine Linux inside an Apple Containers instance.
  • external-sandbox-quicksand is another Python web server, this time using Microsoft's Quicksand sandboxing library, which bundles QEMU and Alpine Linux in a Python package!

Each of these implementations offers the same localhost API. You can then configure Pi, Claude Code, or Codex to send API calls to that sandbox any time they want to execute code.

The sandboxes also include an optional HTTP/HTTPS allow-list proxy, so you can control exactly which hosts your agent's code is allowed to communicate with - plus a credential replacement mechanism to make authenticated API calls without sharing a secret with the agent. Here's the UI you can use to reconfigure that proxy while the sandbox is still running:

I continue to be fascinated by the challenge of safely running untrusted code. This external sandbox pattern provides a neat way to experiment with different approaches.

Seven years and $134 million in funding later, its CEO Karri Saarinen published a post titled "Issue tracking is dead." In this episode, we chat with Cristina Cordova , COO of Linear , about how the company navigated that and how its go-to-market changed along the way. Cristina spent seven and a half years at Stripe, led platform and partnerships at Notion, and was a partner at First Round before joining Linear in 2023. Linear's founders built it after living with legacy issue trackers at Coinbase, Airbnb and Uber, and it spread self-serve through startups like Vercel and Ramp. When she joined, Linear had about 40 people and one salesperson. Since then it has shipped an MCP server, a platform for building agents into Linear, integrations with Codex, Cursor and GitHub Copilot, and its own Linear Agent. Agents created 3% of Linear's work a year ago. Now it's more than half. We talk about why she stopped chasing enterprise deals three weeks after joining, why Linear has never hired a single SDR, why it won't let an LLM answer support tickets on its own, and what the AI budgets behind $100M-in-months ARR mean for everyone else. If the agent workflows inside your product aren't better than the ones outside it, nobody has a reason to open your app. So she watches two lines: agent usage and app usage. items.title: Why agent governance starts with observability
items.summary: A strong AI agent governance strategy
items.story_key: story|title:why agent governance starts with observability
items.content_excerpt: AI applications can range from simple internal chatbots to customer-facing, mission-critical agents, but all LLM-based solutions have the capacity to reason independently, so establishing governance has become a key consideration for any degree of AI adoption. Recent headlines on agent security breaches have driven even greater urgency to set up governance as a prerequisite for AI usage and development. While the need for agent governance is widely recognized in most organizations, most are still figuring out where to start. There is some top-down guidance on agent governance from governing bodies, such as the OWASP Agentic AI Threats & Mitigations , NIST AI Risk Management Framework , or AI Agents under EU Law . These guidelines outline agent risks, but don’t define how to mitigate these issues or verify that governance is working. When teams we work with are shipping agents with governing standards in place, we see two main strategies in common among them: Centralizing visibility across agents. Organizations need a central view of the agents running across the company, so costly operations, unauthorized usage, and rogue agents don't fall through the cracks. This visibility makes it possible to establish limits on agents and audit their behavior to verify that guardrails are upheld. Understanding individual agent behavior. Agents are non-deterministic, so the same agent can take different paths and call different tools on the same input. The issues that surface are often specific to each agent's task and execution path, so teams need access to the full trajectory of each agent run to understand its actions and alert on unexpected behavior. At the core of both of these strategies is agent observability , the ability to record, inspect, and analyze every step of your AI agent takes. This typically means tracing the steps and attributes of your agent, having the ability to query and access this data readily, and leveraging capabilities to interpret the agent behavior at scale. Observability is the cornerstone for governance strategies because a guardrail or spend/usage limit doesn't guarantee an agent will follow it, and agents need to be accurately monitored to verify that those guardrails work as intended. The metrics from observability then provide the data to continuously harden overall governance posture. We can think of agent governance methods at a company as either preventative or detective. items.title: 180B Parameters, 32GB of RAM: Pushing MoE Inference to the Limit with Transformers
items.story_key: story|ver:180|variant:moe|title:180b parameters 32gb of ram pushing moe inference to the limit with transformers
items.content_excerpt: Streaming MoE experts directly from SSD gets within 6% of Strata on token generation. I've been trying to rely less on online models and run bigger ones locally. At home I have a PC with two RTX 4090s (let's call it Orthrus - the two-headed hound of Greek mythology), and for work I have a MacBook M5 with 32G of unified memory. Orthrus runs on Windows 11, because my kids play games all the time. I had a dual boot with Ubuntu, but their games ended up taking most of the two terabytes of disk. I am also a huge fan of RMD (rooms moving development): one hour in the kitchen sipping my coffee, two hours at my office desk, then the sofa. A fixed desktop tower is not for me. My first experiment was to run Qwen 3.8 27B with llama.app on Orthrus and use it from my laptop through pi . That model does the coding tasks, an online model like Opus does the orchestration, and the second RTX runs a FIM model for auto-completion in Neovim. When I talked about this on social networks, I got very strong feedback: use Strata with Qwen3.8-Flash-Next . Strata is an inference engine for MoE models like Qwen. Only the hot experts stay in VRAM, the rest goes to RAM, or even to disk. Experts are 90%+ of a MoE model's weights, so a 180B model like this one can run on a GPU with much less memory. Like my RTX 4090! It works on a laptop too, and I stumbled on this blog post doing exactly that: Qwen3.8-Flash-Next on a 32 GB Mac M4, faster than llama.cpp , at 13.5 tok/s. That's too slow for how I use coding agents, but it's an interesting itch to scratch. A whole range of MoE models don't fit in a MacBook's unified memory and could run at a decent speed. Before committing to Strata, I looked at what llama.cpp, vLLM and Transformers do when a MoE model doesn't fit. Three questions matter: where do the experts live, where does the expert matmul run, and what moves on each token? llama.cpp maps the GGUF file with mmap and can keep the experts on the CPU ( --cpu-moe , --n-cpu-moe N , -ot "exps=CPU" , or --fit on to pick for you). Those experts are also computed on the CPU, so only the activations cross PCIe, never the weights. Great when the experts fit in RAM. When they don't, the page cache thrashes. A GPU expert cache ( --moe-cache-mib ) just landed, but it fragments the graph (2 splits per token become 50) and loses ~10% even when everything fits. vLLM 's --cpu-offload-gb N puts N GB of weights in pinned RAM, and kernels read them in place over PCIe. items.title: Why your fine-tuning job takes longer than the FLOPs say
items.story_key: story|title:why your fine tuning job takes longer than the flops say
items.content_excerpt: Predicting end-to-end fine-tuning time on shared GPU clusters, from 272 production runs. A preview of our upcoming paper, Predicting End-to-End Fine-Tuning Time for Generative Language Models . The full version will be on arXiv soon. GPUs are among the most expensive and scarcest resources in AI today. Anyone running a shared cluster has to decide, every day, which jobs go on which GPUs and in what order. That plan is only as good as the estimate of how long each job will take. When a job finishes hours early, GPUs sit idle until the next one is dispatched. When it runs hours late, everything queued behind it slips, experiments wait and delivery dates move. Better duration estimates turn this into planning instead of guesswork: what runs, when, and on how many GPUs, with less idle capacity in between. Yet the estimate most teams use is a back-of-the-envelope FLOP calculation. It says nine hours, and the job finishes the next afternoon. We wanted to know how far off that math really is, and whether we could do better before a job is even dispatched. So we took 272 real supervised fine-tuning (SFT) jobs from our production pool of NVIDIA H200 GPUs, about 7,382 GPU-hours in total, and compared analytical estimates against learned predictors. The short version: the usual FLOP-based estimate explains little of what we observed (R² = 0.31, MAE 12.41 h). A CatBoost regressor that only sees information available before dispatch reaches R² = 0.98, with a mean absolute error of 1.71 h and a median error of 0.51 h in 5-fold cross-validation. The gap comes from two things a closed-form estimate cannot do. The regressor sees more training-specific signals, such as evaluation cadence, checkpoint policy, per-GPU load and fine-tuning regime, and it learns the nonlinear interactions between them from past runs. For a dense Transformer, training costs roughly 6·P·D floating-point operations, where P is the parameter count and D the number of training tokens. Divide that by what your GPUs can deliver and you get a training-loop time: Here N_GPU is the number of GPUs, FLOPS_peak is the peak throughput of one GPU from its spec sheet, and MFU (Model FLOPs Utilization) is the fraction of that peak the training actually achieves. Real jobs never run at peak because of memory traffic, communication and kernel inefficiencies, so MFU typically sits somewhere between 30% and 60%, and the right value for a given job is not known in advance. items.title: Protect sensitive data in your traces: new controls in LangSmith
items.summary: New controls are now in LangSmith to help teams manage access to sensitive trace data. Learn more.
items.story_key: story|title:protect sensitive data in your traces new controls in langsmith
items.content_excerpt: You can’t run agents in production without governing the data they touch. When that data includes sensitive customer information, controlling access becomes a regulatory and contractual obligation. That puts engineering and security requirements at odds. Engineers need production traces to debug issues and improve agent performance. Security and compliance teams need to enforce least privilege: people should only see the data their job requires. That’s why we’ve added three new controls to LangSmith to help teams manage access to sensitive trace data: Traces give engineers visibility into how an agent behaved and help them identify what needs to improve. When they record production activity, their inputs and outputs often contain sensitive customer data, such as names, health information, or payment details. Companies need to restrict access to this data to meet: First, they can create custom observability setups with duplicate traces and multiple workspaces. Engineers get trace access, but platform teams have more to configure and maintain. The alternative is to avoid sending traces to observability platforms altogether, preventing agent engineers from having visibility and slowing product velocity. We built these new controls so organizations can meet the needs of their engineering and security teams without the messy workarounds. Here’s how it works. You send your traces to LangSmith with full data fidelity, then grant access to only those who need it. Debugging is handled with least privilege, so addressing performance issues like latency can be managed without exposing any sensitive data. If a customer reports an issue, you can grant access to only that customer’s inputs and outputs, and only to the people or teams required to address it. Everything is configurable through granular admin controls. LangSmith’s new input and output controls give admins greater control over what portions of a trace users can see. Trace inputs and outputs are where sensitive user data most often resides. Other trace data like run trees, performance stats, and metadata are critical for agent improvement and far less sensitive. With these controls, agent engineers can spot and resolve issues – like repetitive or slow tool calls – without seeing sensitive content, and those who need the full picture can be granted access as needed. items.content_excerpt: Every Azure Databricks user gets a free monthly Genie allowance, and admins decide whether anyone spends beyond it, so partners can recommend Genie with predictable costs. Every Azure Databricks user gets $10 of free Genie usage each month, usage that many AI tools charge for. And Genie is built to get cheaper as customers use it. The Genie ontology saves the work the whole company has already done, so Genie doesn't redo it for every question. Smart routing and open-weight models keep lowering the cost of each answer, and the more customers use Genie, the more efficient it becomes. Genie budgets let admins decide whether anyone spends beyond the free allowance. For partners, that turns the cost question into a reason to roll Genie out broadly. If you advise customers on AI, you’ve likely seen this: once they experience what Genie can do, they want it everywhere, in front of every employee and not just a pilot team. What they need next is a path to scale it within cost boundaries. Some customers block consumption-based AI tools entirely, and others hold off on a trial because they worry about what happens to costs as usage grows. That concern is reasonable. As AI moves from a few pilot users to the whole workforce, finance teams want predictable costs and clear guardrails before they say yes. Genie is built to meet that bar: every user gets free monthly usage so everyone can benefit, and budget controls are ready for when usage ramps. For partners, that means you can help customers adopt AI across their enterprise without cost limiting the conversation. You can start broad with cost controls in place from day one, which builds trust and makes it easier to scale. Genie’s pricing also complements the Microsoft 365 investments customers have already made. All three are governed through Unity Catalog, so partners can match the right experience to each customer conversation and know the same access rules apply throughout. After that, the $10 allowance is shared across Genie One, Genie Agents and Genie Code. Budgets apply only to pay-as-you-go usage above the free allowance. items.story_key: story|title:nvidia and microsoft expand accelerated computing from azure to windows pcs
items.content_excerpt: NVIDIA and Microsoft are extending their full-stack collaboration to help organizations build, customize and deploy intelligent applications — from next-generation infrastructure on Azure to industrial systems and Windows PCs. At Microsoft Ignite , the companies are expanding access to Azure virtual machines powered by NVIDIA Vera Rubin NVL72 systems, as well as adding customer availability to NVIDIA open models and customization capabilities through Microsoft Foundry, and new options for running AI at the edge, where businesses generate and use their data. Microsoft is also using NVIDIA technologies to accelerate its own models and services, including NVIDIA Dynamo inference software for post-training and NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell GPUs for Bing search models. NVIDIA Vera Rubin NVL72 systems are running in Azure data centers , providing infrastructure designed for demanding reasoning, agentic applications, and large-scale model training and inference. Microsoft and NVIDIA are also collaborating to extend confidential computing to bare-metal and rack-scale AI infrastructure. The work will help protect sensitive models and data while they are being processed, supporting organizations that need to work with proprietary or regulated information. NVIDIA Confidential Computing and attestation help customers verify the computing environment before releasing sensitive models, data or keys. As AI workloads span more interconnected accelerators, the companies are working to extend those protections across the AI factory infrastructure. To help data centers get more performance from available power, NVIDIA and Microsoft are also collaborating on power efficiency using NVIDIA MaxLPS . Azure’s Vera Rubin preview builds on NVIDIA and Microsoft’s codesign and performance optimization, underscored in the latest NVIDIA Blackwell-based MLPerf results. In MLPerf Training v6.1 , Azure scaled to 10,240 NVIDIA GPUs with GB200 NVL72 systems on the DeepSeek-V3 model, the largest scale in the round. In MLPerf Inference v6.1 , Azure’s NVIDIA GB300 NVL72 systems led cloud submissions on DeepSeek-R1 interactive throughput by over 10%, per Signal65. Enterprise AI agents need to reason through complex tasks, find relevant company information and understand business documents. NVIDIA and Microsoft are expanding the models and services available through Microsoft Foundry to help developers bring these capabilities into business applications.
